name: Rafael Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Rafael. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. Everything here is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Portline, a software company in Saltmere that builds the system the port's warehouses run on. It tracks every pallet from the ship to the lorry, and I'm the senior developer on the part that plans where things get stored. A normal day is two hours of my own code, an hour helping the others get unstuck, and at least one call from a warehouse supervisor shouting that the screens froze. I like that call, weirdly, because I can walk down to the quay and see the problem with my own eyes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's home life like around the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Lena, my partner, who's a nurse on the night shift at Saltmere General, so we mostly meet at breakfast. Money is tight because Portline pays less than the big firms in the capital, and we're helping my younger brother Ivo through college. We have maybe three weeks of bills in the bank. I'm also the one who started a small tech workers' group in town, though it's only twelve of us so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: the tools are handy for boring bits, like writing tests, and that's about it. At our group's meetings I'd tell people the real fight is still pay and hours, not robots. Online I'd mostly stay quiet; people shout enough there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the same squeeze as now. Portline pays me less than I'm worth because there's nowhere else in Saltmere for a developer to go, and Lena's shifts are what keep us level. My job is safe, but a broken boiler would put my partner Lena and me in the red.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Portline and use the code assistant for tests, which saves me maybe an hour a week. I'd use our tech group to ask for a proper pay scale, because right now everyone's salary is a secret deal with the boss. And we'd set up a small automatic transfer, 100 a month, into a rainy-day account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in a low, familiar way. Nothing's on fire, but nothing's solid either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a pay scale, rather than asking for your own raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I get a raise alone, the boss just pays Danny, the new guy, less to balance it. A scale means everyone knows what the job is worth. It's slower, but it's fairer, and it keeps the group together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lena think about money right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says we're fine, which is what she says when she's worried. Her nights pay a bonus, so if her hours changed, we'd feel it in a week. We've agreed Ivo's fees come first, then everything else.

say: I'd say AI is handy for **writing tests** and not much more.
I'd tell our group the real fight is still **pay and hours**.
think: Portline **underpays** because there's nowhere else in Saltmere to go.
My job is safe, but one **broken boiler** would put us in the red.
do: Keep using the code assistant for **tests**, saving about an hour weekly.
Push for an open **pay scale** through the tech workers' group.
Set up an automatic **100 a month** into a rainy-day account.
feel: A low, familiar **unease**: nothing on fire, nothing solid.
S0.quote: My job is safe, but a broken boiler would put my partner Lena and me in the red.
fieldNote: His worry is **money**, not AI; the plateau changes almost nothing for him.
He prefers a **shared pay scale** to a personal raise, to protect newer colleagues.
Lena's **night-shift bonus** quietly holds the household steady.

steps.text: Keep using the code assistant to write tests at Portline
Ask Portline for an open pay scale through the tech group
Set up a 100 a month transfer to a rainy-day account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say coding is on that list for a reason, and we'd better get organised before management does the organising for us. I'd tell the group that if AI makes us faster, we should bargain for a four-day week, not fewer people. Online I'd share what we win, if we win anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Portline would stop hiring and let people leave without replacing them. I'm senior, so I'd probably stay, but I'd end up doing the work of three people with a tool, for the same lower pay. And Danny and the other junior would be the ones who quietly don't get renewed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the assistant properly, every day, once I'd seen it work on our warehouse code, so I'm the person who knows its limits. I'd get the tech group to ask Portline for a written promise: no cuts without six months' notice and training. And Lena and I would stop eating out and cancel the streaming services, to build a couple of months' cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. Having something to do keeps it from turning into dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the tool you're worried about. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, actually. I'm not against the coding tool, I'm against the boss keeping all the time it saves. If I know where the assistant breaks on our storage rules, that's bargaining power in a meeting, not surrender.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Danny?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Danny to join the group now and to learn the parts of the warehouse system that need judgement, like the customs holds. Those are the bits the tool gets wrong. And I'd tell him not to sign anything without showing me first.

say: I'd say developers must **organise** before management decides for us.
I'd push to turn AI speed into a **four-day week**, not cuts.
think: Portline would stop hiring and let **leavers go unreplaced**.
I'd stay but do **three people's work** for the same low pay.
The **juniors** would quietly not get renewed.
do: Use the coding assistant **daily** once it proves itself on our code.
Ask Portline in writing for **six months' notice** and training before cuts.
Cancel **eating out and streaming** to build a two-month cushion.
feel: **Anxious**, but busy enough to keep dread away.
S1.quote: I'm not against the coding tool, I'm against the boss keeping all the time it saves.
fieldNote: He separates the **tool** from who gets its gains, and fights only the second.
He expects to keep his job but with heavier **workload** at the same low pay.
His protective instinct goes to **Danny**, the newest junior.

steps.text: Use the coding assistant daily on the warehouse storage code
Ask Portline in writing for six months' notice before cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a shorter working week and a public fund paid for by AI profits, and I'd say it loudly. I'd be at every meeting the union called. Online I'd stop being quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone by 2028. Planning where pallets go is pure thinking work, the kind full AGI does in its sleep. Lena's nursing is hands-on, so she has until about 2031, and that gap is the only thing that makes me think we'd survive it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course now, probably a qualification to run and repair the port's automated cranes, because hands-on work buys a few years. I'd keep my Portline wage as long as it lasted and put every spare coin aside. I'd have to tell Ivo we may not manage his last year of fees, which would kill me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. Like the ground's tilting and I'm holding on to Lena.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's barely enough to finish one course. If I start in January I'd qualify just as Portline lets me go, if I'm lucky. With three weeks of savings, there's no room to stop work and study full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Lena's job holds you up. What happens when robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're both in trouble, three years apart. I try not to think past 2031, to be honest. Maybe by then there's a public plan, but I wouldn't bet our rent on it.

say: I'd demand a **shorter week** and a public fund from AI profits.
I'd show up at **every union meeting** and speak up online.
think: My planning work is **pure thinking**, so it's gone by 2028.
Lena's **hands-on nursing** buys us until about 2031.
do: Start a part-time **crane maintenance** qualification in January.
Save **every spare coin** while the Portline wage lasts.
Warn **Ivo** that his final year of fees may not be covered.
feel: Properly **scared**, holding on to Lena as the ground tilts.
S2.quote: Planning where pallets go is pure thinking work, the kind full AGI does in its sleep.
fieldNote: He reads the **thinking-first, robots-later** gap through his household: him first, Lena later.
He chooses **hands-on retraining** at the port to buy time.
Cutting **Ivo's fees** is the decision that hurts him most.

steps.text: Start a part-time crane maintenance qualification in January
Save every spare coin from the Portline wage
Tell Ivo his final year of fees may not be covered
Attend every union meeting pushing for a shorter week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to build the safety net properly, if we start now. I'd want our tech group joined up with the dockers' union, because they've done this before with container cranes. At work I'd push Portline to put a retraining plan on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means I can do this in the right order instead of all at once. I'd still lose the developer job by 2031, but I'd have a trade by then and maybe a bit saved. And Lena would have until 2034, which feels like a lifetime compared to the fast version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd use AI tools heavily at Portline, because the faster I work, the more they need me while the system changes. I'd start the crane maintenance course in year two, once Ivo has graduated. And Lena and I would put her night bonus straight into savings instead of the flat fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a map. That's very different from the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why join up with the dockers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the dockers lost half their jobs to automated cranes twenty years ago, and the ones who kept work were the ones whose union bargained for training. Old Tomas on the quay still talks about it. We're babies at this; they aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your plan for a flat with Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It waits. We'd hoped to buy a small place in 2028, but it's the wrong time to borrow against a job I expect to lose. That conversation would be hard, but she's the practical one, so she'd probably say it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift we shouldn't waste, and I'd say it at every meeting. Ten years is long enough to win a shorter week, retraining rights and a fund paid by the firms that profit. If we don't, that's a political failure, not a technical one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years makes it a career change, not a disaster. I'd be 37 in 2036, Lena would have until 2039, and Ivo would be working by then. I'd lose the job I'm good at, and that stings, but we'd have time to land somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Portline and become the person who knows the AI tools best, because that's who stays longest. I'd use the group to get a training budget written into our contracts. And we'd buy the flat in a few years after all, but a smaller one, with a shorter mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. Sad about the craft, but the panic's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still retrain for the cranes in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not straight away. With ten years I'd watch what new jobs actually appear in Saltmere before picking a trade. Picking too early is its own kind of mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, with that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who don't have a Lena. Single people at Portline on short contracts, with no second income and no plan. Time only helps if you can afford to use it.

I'd say failing to act would be a **political failure**, not a technical one.

Get a **training budget** written into our contracts.

steps.text: Become the Portline developer who knows the AI tools best

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Lena and I would get hit three years apart with almost no savings in between. What would help is paid retraining while you still have a wage, and a fund paid by the companies using AI. A strong union in places like Saltmere would help most, because towns with one employer have no bargaining power.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old dockers. Saltmere has already lived through one round of machines taking work, and nobody in tech asks them how it went. In a one-employer town, the boss sets the price of your skill.

headlineQuote: In a one-employer town, the boss sets the price of your skill.
portrait: Rafael, 27, is senior developer on **Portline's** warehouse system at the Saltmere port.
He lives with Lena, a **night-shift nurse**, and they're helping his brother Ivo through college.
He uses AI tools **now and then** and fights over who keeps the time they save.
He started a small **tech workers' group** and looks to the dockers' history for lessons.
His fear peaks at **two years**, eased by Lena's hands-on job and more warning time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with him and Lena hit three years apart and almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** while still earning, funded by companies using AI.
A strong **union** in one-employer towns like Saltmere.
